positions.commentary: Brian Armstrong believes that great companies are often built in down markets because there is no distraction and founders can build back up from a low point.

thesis: This episode argues that going public legitimized Coinbase for institutional integration but introduced the drawback of daily stock marking, creating a mixed experience for the founder. It further advises founders to maintain control via dual-class structures, cut costs early rather than during downturns, and view down markets as opportunities to build great companies without distraction.

claims.claim: Brian Armstrong states that going public legitimized Coinbase as a company, allowing major firms like BlackRock, Meta, and Google to integrate with them.
claims.quote: It legitimized us as a company. It was kind of a great marketing thing. And then also other Fortune 500 companies suddenly started to take us seriously, right? So we closed these deals with BlackRock, like the biggest asset manager in the world, and like meta and Google.

claims.claim: Brian Armstrong notes that while being public makes raising money easier, the daily marking to market of the stock is a serious drawback.
claims.quote: The pros are, there's a handful of things. One, it's a lot easier to raise money. Like, actually, in 2021, Coinbase raised $3 billion of debt in, you know, with very favorable terms. I didn't do a single meeting. our CFO did it. It took a week. And the money was in our account. So somehow, as a public company, you just have access to all these. You can't do that as a private company, just FYI. Yea

claims.claim: Brian Armstrong admits that while he initially hoped to go public, he was skeptical because he feared losing control, but the experience has been mixed with pros and cons.
claims.quote: But I always thought, ah, being a public company, that's where you lose control. And, you know, I was basically pretty skeptical of it. And so as we got to be bigger, I started to do some research. I went and talked to a bunch of CEOs who had decided to stay private or they'd brought in a professional CEO to take it public or something or something had actually gone public, right? And look, there'

claims.claim: Brian Armstrong mentions that Coinbase's stock has gone down significantly along with other high growth tech stocks in the current environment.
claims.quote: And so, you know, everybody can see our revenue multiples and stuff and it were, you know, it's, it's not great. Like, our stock is down quite a lot with any kind of high growth tech stock in this environment is down quite a lot.

claims.claim: Brian Armstrong states that spending time with public market investors was not as time-consuming as he worried, and he has built good relationships with them.
claims.quote: I was worried about this idea of, you know, I was going to have to spend like 20, 30, 40 percent of my time speaking with public market investors. I don't, that turned out to not really be the case. I think I basically, you know, I do the earnings calls. We have a couple times a year in each, each quarter where I go spend time with public market investors. I've started to build good relationships

claims.claim: Brian Armstrong advises founders to learn about dual class stock to maintain control against activist investors, noting that Coinbase uses this structure.
claims.quote: The last thing I'll say is that dual class stock is it is something people should go learn about. And everyone has their own opinion on that of, you know, basically you can have a different class of shares that allow you to still maintain control so you're not dealing with kind of activist investors constantly, which for me was a good factor that allowed me to sort of focus on the stuff I'm good a

claims.claim: Brian Armstrong suggests that founders should not cut costs too soon during a downturn, but rather cut up front to capture savings earlier.
claims.quote: So traps that we've companies fall into in down in crypto cycles. Yeah, I mean, I think, I don't know, the most common one I see is that, you know, we're just going to, basically they don't cut costs soon enough, right? And it's harder if you wait, you have to cut more. And if you do it up front, you can basically capture some of the savings, you know, earlier on.

claims.claim: Brian Armstrong advises founders to flip their mentality from pessimism and fear to seeing opportunities in every down market.
claims.quote: And then the other trick is basically flip your mentality from, you know, pessimism and fear and scarcity to, how is this actually an opportunity, right? And there actually always is an opportunity in every down market. And that's the next mindset to get.
